en.gtgr_desc: Teaching a computer my accent, and finding out I don’t spell it the same way twice.
en.gtgr_h3_why-cmudict-still-disagrees: Why CMUdict still disagrees with me
en.gtgr_h3_rules-i-didnt-know-i-had: Rules I didn’t know I had
en.gtgr_p1: Graflect is phonic: you spell what you say. So if a computer knows how I talk, it should be able to write Graflect for me. To find out how close one gets, every Graflect article on this site becomes a test. The computer studies all of my other articles, gets only the English of the one left out, and spells it. Then it’s scored on how many words it spelled the way I did.
en.gtgr_p2: The system has two parts. First, my own words: anything I’ve already written in another article gets spelled the same way again. Second, CMUdict, a pronunciation dictionary of American English, put through my rules: tr is cr, dr is jr, a before n and m is ä, and so on. Two more rules look at the next word: “the” is dhī before a vowel, and “have to” is hæf tü. Right now it spells 92.7% of my words the way I did.
en.gtgr_p3: Most of that is my own words coming back. CMUdict carries a fifth of it, all on words I’ve only ever written in one article.
en.gtgr_p4: Here is every version, in order. Each bar is every word in my Graflect articles at the time: the open part is the words spelled the way I did, and the patterned part is the misses, sorted by why. v0 is the site before any of this: my hand-made dictionary, which spelled 45% of my words right and left everything else in Latin.
en.gtgr_ol1:
• v0, 18 Nov 17:15: my hand-made dictionary, 44.9%. The converter this site already had. It knew a couple hundred common words; the other 2,859 stayed in Latin.
  • v1, 18 Nov 22:34: words from my other articles, 64.3%. Anything I had already written in another article gets spelled the same way again.
  • v2, 18 Nov 23:07: the dictionary follows my articles, 67.5%. Where my dictionary and my articles disagreed, the articles won.
  • v3, 18 Nov 23:22: more of the same, 68.0%. very, even, people, man, than.
  • v4, 18 Nov 23:29: because, what, we, 68.6%. Three common words my articles spelled differently from the dictionary.
  • v5, 19 Nov 02:09: CMUdict through my rules, 85.6%. Every word CMUdict knows gets spelled by my rules. Unknown words fell from 1,628 to 92. Now the misses are CMUdict disagreeing with me (409), and me disagreeing with myself (220).
  • v6, 19 Nov 02:16: tr-words keep the r, 85.8%. crip, crai, cränzlēt. I had been dropping the r after c.
  • v7, 19 Nov 04:09: fixes from the P40 report, 87.4%. “The” before a vowel became its own rule, words I usually leave in Latin stay in Latin, dr keeps its r (jr), and I fixed have, had and think in my articles.
  • v8, 19 Nov 04:53: ä, īng, no apostrophes, 88.9%. ä before n and m (can, man, hand), -ing is īng, and no apostrophes inside Graflect words: Graflect is phonic. All 60 apostrophe misses, gone.
  • v9, 19 Nov 06:17: proofreading round 1, 90.3%. 178 words where CMUdict and I disagreed, or where I had spelled a word more than one way. I changed 91. Me disagreeing with myself fell from 115 to 58.
  • v10, 19 Nov 06:35: slips, and a bug, 90.7%. grælekt, kībõrdz, and “half” written as have. The bug: the converter had started writing “there” as dh·4, two glyphs where I write one.
  • v11, 19 Nov 15:41: -ing is īngg, 90.8%. Every -ing gets its g. 206 words in my articles changed, but the converter changed to match, so the score barely moved.
  • v12, 19 Nov 16:48: the wī glyph, 90.8%. w then ī is always the wī glyph: wī, wīl, wīk.
  • v13, 19 Nov 17:24: the unstressed vowel, 92.2%. The report showed I write i, not x, before a final d, z, n, t or s: ēdid, srvisiz, gárdin, edit. Also a bug (r and ä were read back as the single rä glyph) and seven places that broke my own rules for “the” and “have to”.
  • v14, 19 Nov 17:52: CMUdict’s other pronunciations, 92.7%. Where CMUdict lists more than one way to say a word, take the one with i in an unstressed syllable, like I say it. And “the” is dhī before a name I keep in Latin that starts with a vowel: dhī Iris.
en.gtgr_ul1:
• CMUdict ≠ me, 248. 135 of these are only the unstressed vowel, x or i. The rest are how I talk: dikšin4ī, lēngwijiz, sfīr, práblim.
  • Unknown words, 94. Not in CMUdict, and not in my other articles: pinkies, glyphs, encoders, plushies.
  • Me ≠ me, 50. Words that depend on context (read, use, a as x or ē), and 21 words I usually leave in Latin, like system and program, that I spelled out once.
  • Structure and context, 29. Lines where I rewrote the sentence instead of transliterating it.
  • Another CMUdict pronunciation, 23. CMUdict lists another pronunciation that matches mine (rescránt, dītēl), and the system picked a different one.
en.gtgr_p5: CMUdict is a list of how 126,000 words are said in General American English, made at Carnegie Mellon. It’s a fixed file, and I don’t edit it: it goes through my rules, and where it knows more than one pronunciation, the system picks the one closest to mine. What’s left isn’t CMUdict being wrong, or me being wrong. CMUdict writes almost every unstressed vowel the same way, where I choose between x and i, and the rest is my accent. Every one of those words is in only one of my articles, so the system has never seen me spell it.
en.gtgr_ul2:
• “The” is dhx, but dhī before a vowel, even in a name I keep in Latin.
  • “A” is x, and ē when I stress it.
  • “And” is änd, but xnd in set pairs like “cookies and cream”.
  • “Have to” is hæf tü.
  • Every -ing has its g: thīngg, yüzīngg.
  • w then ī is the wī glyph: wī, wīl, wīk.
  • The unstressed vowel is i before a final d, z, n, t or s, and x before l, m and p.
en.gtgr_p6: Next, a small neural network trained on Geniza, my home server, with an Nvidia P40. It learns pronunciation from CMUdict first, then my spellings, and it only gets the words the rules can’t handle: the unknown words, and maybe the vowel. Its first run guessed 65% of dictionary words it had never seen exactly right, and added 39 words to the rules’ score. Now that my articles agree with themselves, it’s time to train it again.
